description: Solo entry for Dancing with the SARs, using NISAR radar data to track and visualize surface change on an interactive map.
summary: GeoSentinel is an interactive Earth-observation application developed by Adel S Al Lahibi of Band of One for Dancing with the SARs. It investigates changing water extent at Navajo Reservoir using NISAR radar, Sentinel-2 imagery and official reservoir records. Users compare dates, inspect water candidates and explore ambiguous areas. Optical candidates expand by 9.75–10.41 square kilometres across tested thresholds. Radar model candidates increase by 14.77 square kilometres, but 71% of this net increase comes from net exchange with the ambiguous class. Most ambiguous-to-water pixels overlap persistent optical-water candidates rather than new optical gains. These findings reveal how classification and acquisition timing affect apparent change. GeoSentinel supports shoreline inspection, research and education through an interactive viewer, documented code and reproducible results. Independent shoreline validation remains outstanding.
details:
GeoSentinel was developed and revised by Adel S Al Lahibi of Band of One for Dancing with the SARs.

The project investigates changing water extent at Navajo Reservoir using NISAR GCOV HH/HV observations from 26 October and 7 November 2026. Sentinel-2 imagery from 27 October and 11 November provides optical context, with acquisition-time differences explicitly documented. Historical USGS NHD geometry provides a spatial reference, while provisional USBR reservoir observations support interpretation.

The interactive HTML, CSS and JavaScript viewer provides a draggable comparison, full-date views, radar candidate gains and losses, and controls for inspecting ambiguous areas. Display filters do not change the analytical totals.

Python processing uses NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, h5py, Matplotlib and supporting libraries. The workflow includes quality screening, grid alignment, optical threshold sensitivity and a conservative radar model that retains an ambiguous class.

The project helps reservoir managers prioritize shoreline checks and helps researchers and educators understand radar uncertainty. Its distinctive feature is making differences between sensors, dates and classification choices visible rather than presenting one definitive water-area estimate.

Independent shoreline validation, terrain assessment and noise normalization remain outstanding. GeoSentinel is an exploratory research application, not an operational flood-warning system.

AI tools assisted with writing and reviewing some code and preparing documentation drafts. Satellite observations came from the cited providers and were not AI-generated. The package includes an AI assistance disclosure and metadata.
